I didn't realize that Denmark's borders had been defined so recently. TIL.

The historical reason is "kingdoms and duchies" moreso than anything.

Ever since pretty much the viking-middle ages, the border ran further south to include all of Schleswig and Holstein, it looked more like this (if we don't include Skåneland), but the area has always had a higher number of German-speaking people than Danish-speaking people.

This cultural difference became apparent as the concept of a German nation sprouted, and the territory changed hands back and forth, until the end of World War 1, when a new dividing line was drawn along northern Schleswig in accordance with the plebiscite and the map shown in this post.
